items.stem: Under the shared-responsibility model for IaaS, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?

options.rationale: Correct: in IaaS the customer manages the OS and above.
The provider secures the underlying infrastructure, not the guest OS in IaaS.
OS patching is a managed responsibility, not automatic here.

options.text: The end users of the application
options.rationale: End users do not patch the server OS.

items.explanation: Correct: in IaaS the customer is responsible for the guest OS.

items.stem: Which TWO practices reduce cloud identity risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Granting least-privilege roles instead of broad admin
options.rationale: Correct: least privilege limits the blast radius of a compromise.

options.text: Using short-lived credentials or a secrets manager
options.rationale: Correct: short-lived secrets reduce the value of stolen keys.

options.text: Sharing one root key across the whole team
options.rationale: A shared root key removes accountability and widens risk.

options.text: Embedding long-lived keys in public code
options.rationale: Hard-coded keys in public code are frequently stolen.

items.explanation: Correct: least privilege and short-lived credentials both cut identity risk.

items.stem: A storage bucket holding customer files is world-readable. What is the best remediation?

options.text: Restrict access to only the identities that require it and audit the exposure
options.rationale: Correct: least-privilege access plus reviewing who accessed it addresses the exposure.

options.text: Rename the bucket and leave it public
options.rationale: Renaming does not remove public access.

options.text: Delete the logging so the issue is not recorded
options.rationale: Removing logs hides evidence and worsens posture.

options.text: Make every other bucket public too for consistency
options.rationale: This spreads the exposure instead of fixing it.

items.explanation: Correct: restrict to required identities and audit the exposure.
